implementation_notes: Swift has the value holder in the language: a lazy stored property's initial value is not calculated until the first time the property is used, and it is stored afterwards, so 'lazy var author: Author = gateway.find(authorID)' is the lazy-initialization form; the initializer may reference self and other stored properties, which is why a lazy property is always a var. What replaces the classic holder/proxy is the keyword; for values that must be reloaded or whose load can fail, a throwing method plus a private optional cache is the right shape, because a lazy initializer is evaluated exactly once and cannot throw.
pitfalls: lazy var is not single-flight: simultaneous first access from several threads is not guaranteed to initialize only once, so shared objects need a lock or an eagerly built value.
The initializer cannot throw and runs once per instance: a fallible load must be a throwing method or an optional cache, and mutating the input does not invalidate the stored value.
A struct copy carries its own deferral, so an uninitialized lazy property is evaluated on that copy's first access; lazy is also not allowed on let or before all stored properties are initialized.
